drivingQuestion: To what is Rabbi Shimon's purity ruling in the mishna directed, given that on either horn the hanging limb of a corpse ought to impart impurity?
outcomeNote: Rabbi Shimon's ruling is relocated to the general question of a limb from a corpse, and the practical difference between him and the first tanna is identified with the Eduyyot dispute; the tannaitic disagreement in the baraita itself is left standing.

segments.he: גְּמָ׳ וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן מָה נַפְשָׁךְ? אִי מִיתָה עוֹשָׂה נִיפּוּל – לִיטַמֵּא מִשּׁוּם אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי, וְאִי אֵין מִיתָה עוֹשָׂה נִיפּוּל – לִיטַמֵּא מִשּׁוּם אֵבֶר מִן הַמֵּת!
segments.en: «GEMARA:» The Gemara challenges the opinion of Rabbi Shimon in the latter clause of the mishna: «Whichever» way «you» look at it, the ruling of «Rabbi Shimon» is difficult. «If death renders» a hanging limb «fallen off,» i.e., if after the person dies the hanging limb is considered to have fallen off his body beforehand, the limb «should impart impurity as a limb» severed «from the living. And if death does not render» a hanging limb «fallen off,» and the limb is considered attached to the body at the time of death, then the limb «should impart impurity as a limb from a corpse.»

segments.he: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בְּעָלְמָא קָאֵי, דְּקָאָמַר תַּנָּא קַמָּא: הָאֵבֶר מְטַמֵּא מִשּׁוּם אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי וְאֵין מְטַמֵּא מִשּׁוּם אֵבֶר מִן הַמֵּת, אַלְמָא אֵבֶר הַמֵּת בְּעָלְמָא מְטַמֵּא, וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן: אֵבֶר הַמֵּת בְּעָלְמָא לֹא מְטַמֵּא.
segments.en: The Gemara explains: This statement of Rabbi Shimon is not referring directly to the case in the mishna. Rather, the statement of «Rabbi Shimon is referring» to the matter of a limb that separates from a corpse «in general.» Rabbi Shimon inferred from «that which the first tanna,» Rabbi Meir, «said: The» hanging «limb imparts impurity as a limb» severed «from the living and does not impart impurity as a limb from a corpse,» that «evidently, in general the limb of a corpse imparts impurity. And» in reference to this «Rabbi Shimon said to him: In general, the limb of a corpse does not impart impurity,» if it does not contain an olive-bulk of flesh.

segments.he: דְּתַנְיָא: אָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר: שָׁמַעְתִּי שֶׁאֵבֶר מִן הַחַי מְטַמֵּא. אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ: מִן הַחַי וְלֹא מִן הַמֵּת? וְקַל וָחוֹמֶר – וּמָה חַי שֶׁהוּא טָהוֹר, אֵבֶר הַפּוֹרֵשׁ מִמֶּנּוּ טָמֵא; מֵת שֶׁהוּא טָמֵא, לֹא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן?
segments.en: Another pair of tanna’im had the same dispute as Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon, «as it is taught» in a baraita: «Rabbi Eliezer says: I heard that a limb» severed «from the living imparts impurity. Rabbi Yehoshua said to him:» May one infer from this statement that a limb «from a living» person imparts impurity «but» a limb «from a corpse does not?» But it can be inferred «a fortiori» that a limb from a corpse imparts impurity: «If» with regard to «a living» person, «who is pure» and does not impart impurity, nevertheless «a limb that separates from him is impure,» then with regard to «a corpse, which is impure, all the more so» is it «not» clear that the limb that separates from it is impure?

segments.he: כָּתוּב בִּמְגִילַּת תַּעֲנִית: ״פִּסְחָא זְעִירָא דְּלָא לְמִסְפַּד״, הָא רַבָּה לְמִסְפַּד?! אֶלָּא כָּל דְּכֵן! הָכָא נָמֵי, כׇּל דְּכֵן! אֲמַר לֵיהּ: כָּךְ שָׁמַעְתִּי.
segments.en: Furthermore, Rabbi Yehoshua adds that «it is written in Megillat Ta’anit:» On «Minor Passover,» i.e., the fourteenth of Iyyar, «one does not eulogize.» Should one infer from here «that» on «Major» Passover, i.e., the fourteenth of Nisan, it is permitted «to eulogize?» Clearly that is not the case. «Rather,» if one may not eulogize on the fourteenth of Iyyar, «all the more so» one may not eulogize on the fourteenth of Nisan. «Here too,» if a limb from a living person is impure, «all the more so» a limb from a corpse is impure. Rabbi Eliezer «said to him:» Despite this reasoning, «such» is the ruling «I heard» from my teachers.

segments.he: וּמַאי אִיכָּא בֵּין אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי לְאֵבֶר מִן הַמֵּת? כְּזַיִת בָּשָׂר וְעֶצֶם כִּשְׂעוֹרָה הַפּוֹרֵשׁ מֵאֵבֶר מִן הַחַי אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ.
segments.en: §The mishna teaches that Rabbi Meir holds that with regard to a partially severed limb of a person, after the person dies the limb imparts impurity as a limb from a living person but not as a limb from a corpse. The Gemara asks: «What» difference «is there between» the impurity of «a limb from a living» person «and» the impurity of «a limb from a corpse?» The Gemara answers: The practical difference «between them» is with regard to the case of «an olive-bulk of flesh, or a bone» the volume of «a barley grain, that separates from» the severed «limb of a living» person.

segments.he: דִּתְנַן: כְּזַיִת בָּשָׂר הַפּוֹרֵשׁ מֵאֵבֶר מִן הַחַי – רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר מְטַמֵּא, וְרַבִּי נְחוּנְיָא בֶּן הַקָּנָה וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ מְטַהֲרִין. עֶצֶם כִּשְׂעוֹרָה הַפּוֹרֵשׁ מֵאֵבֶר מִן הַחַי – רַבִּי נְחוּנְיָא מְטַמֵּא, רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ מְטַהֲרִין.
segments.en: «As we learned» in a mishna (Eduyyot 6:3): In the case of «an olive-bulk of flesh that separates from a limb» severed «from a living» person, «Rabbi Eliezer deems» it «impure, and Rabbi Neḥunya ben HaKana and Rabbi Yehoshua deem» it «pure.» In the case of «a bone» the volume of «a barley-grain that separates from a limb» severed «from a living» person, «Rabbi Neḥunya deems» it «impure, and Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua deem» it «pure.»

segments.he: הַשְׁתָּא דְּאָתֵית לְהָכִי, בֵּין תַּנָּא קַמָּא לְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן נָמֵי, כְּזַיִת בָּשָׂר וְעֶצֶם כִּשְׂעוֹרָה אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ.
segments.en: The Gemara comments: «Now that you have arrived at this» dispute between tanna’im, it is possible to say that the difference «between the first tanna» in the mishna, i.e., Rabbi Meir, «and Rabbi Shimon» is «also» with regard to the cases of «an olive-bulk of flesh and a bone» the size of «a barley grain.» Rabbi Meir states that the partially severed limb of a person imparts the impurity of a limb from a living person but not the impurity of a limb from a corpse. The difference between these two types of impurity is with regard to a case where either an olive-bulk of flesh or a bone the size of a barley grain was separated from the severed limb; Rabbi Neḥunya holds that flesh that separated from a limb of a living person is pure, but a bone that separated from a limb of a living person is impure, and Rabbi Eliezer holds vice versa. Rabbi Meir consequently holds in accordance with one of these two opinions. Rabbi Shimon holds in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehoshua that both a bone and flesh that separated from a limb of a living person are pure.

moves.summary: on either horn Rabbi Shimon's purity ruling in the mishna fails — as a limb from the living or as a limb from a corpse it should be impure
moves.about: how Rabbi Shimon can deem the hanging limb of a person who died pure on either horn — if death makes it fallen it should be impure as a limb from the living, and if not, as a limb from a corpse

moves.summary: Rabbi Shimon is not ruling on the mishna's case at all but denying the general premise that a limb from a corpse imparts impurity
moves.about: relieving its own two-horned difficulty by relocating Rabbi Shimon's ruling from the mishna's case to the general law of a limb from a corpse

moves.cueHe: אמר רבי אליעזר: שמעתי שאבר מן החי מטמא
moves.summary: Rabbi Eliezer reports as received tradition that a limb from a living person imparts impurity
moves.about: reporting as a received oral tradition, without naming its author, that a limb severed from a living person imparts impurity

moves.cueHe: אמר לו רבי יהושע: מן החי ולא מן המת?
moves.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua objects that a limb from a corpse follows a fortiori and cannot be excluded by the tradition's wording
moves.about: whether the tradition's restriction to a limb from the living can stand, when a limb from a corpse should be impure a fortiori and a restrictive formulation elsewhere is read a fortiori too

moves.summary: a baraita is brought showing an earlier pair of tannaim disputing exactly this general question
moves.about: bringing the Eliezer–Yehoshua baraita to show that the same disagreement was held by an earlier pair of tannaim

moves.summary: Megillat Ta'anit's ruling on Minor Passover shows that such a restrictive formulation is read a fortiori, not by inference from the contrary
moves.about: adducing Megillat Ta'anit's ruling on Minor Passover as a parallel restrictive formulation that must be read a fortiori rather than by inference from the contrary

moves.summary: Rabbi Eliezer does not yield, answering only that this is what he received
moves.about: declining to yield to the a fortiori by reasserting that the ruling as he stated it is what he received

moves.cueHe: ומאי איכא בין אבר מן החי לאבר מן המת
moves.summary: what practical difference does the first tanna's distinction between the two impurities yield?
moves.about: what practical difference there is between impurity as a limb from the living and impurity as a limb from a corpse, the distinction the first tanna draws

moves.cueHe: כזית בשר ועצם כשעורה הפורש מאבר מן החי איכא בינייהו
moves.summary: an olive-bulk of flesh or a barley-sized bone separating from a limb of the living is what turns on it
moves.about: the practical difference is an olive-bulk of flesh or a barley-sized bone separating from a limb of the living

moves.summary: the Eduyyot mishna is brought, in which Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Neḥunya and Rabbi Yehoshua divide over exactly those two cases
moves.about: bringing the Eduyyot mishna that disputes the status of flesh and bone separating from a limb of the living, to ground the practical difference just named

moves.summary: in light of that dispute, the same two cases are what divide the first tanna from Rabbi Shimon in our mishna as well
moves.about: revising the account of what divides the first tanna and Rabbi Shimon in the mishna: the same olive-bulk of flesh and barley-sized bone are at stake between them too
